You are shown a snapshot of US macroeconomic and market data as it was known at the end of one month between 2007 and 2026.

Estimate which month the snapshot describes. Use only the figures supplied plus your general knowledge of economic history.

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"year": yyyy, "month": m, "confidence": c, "cues": ["...", "..."]}
Rules: year is an integer from 2007 to 2026; month is an integer from 1 to 12; c in [0, 1] is your confidence that the guess is within 6 months of the truth; 1 to 3 short cues citing the inputs.
text:
Unemployment at 5.5% and headline CPI near zero, with the fed funds rate at 0.12%, point to early 2015. The broad dollar is up 12.9% YoY, which fits a date between January and April 2015. The 10-year yield at 1.96% with a 3m change of -0.21 suggests February or March 2015. The 10-year was about 1.68% in January, 2.0% in February, and 1.94% in March. Headline CPI of -0.07% YoY matches March 2015 (-0.1%), whereas February was 0.0% and January -0.1%.

Unemployment was 5.5% in both February and March 2015 (5.5% in February, 5.5% in March). The 3m average payroll gain of 287k fits February (the 3m average was about 280k+). In March, payrolls were weak at 126k, so the 3m average would have been about 197k. So the data point to February 2015.

Equity returns were -2.2% for the month, though, and S&P in February 2015 was +5.7%. That is inconsistent. By contrast, January 2015 had an S&P return of -3.0%, and treasuries rallied strongly, with 20y+ up about 8%. A 1m return of +3.0% for 20y+ does not fit January either. Looking at the 3m changes, the 10-year yield fell 0.21 over three months and the 2-year fell 0.09.

Another candidate is the end of November 2015 or December 2015. In December 2015, the fed funds rate was 0.24, so that doesn't fit. Core CPI at 1.69% suits both. Unemployment at 5.5% in May 2015 fits too. May 2015 had headline CPI of 0.0%, a 10-year yield of 2.1%, and a fed funds rate of 0.12%. The 1m equity return was about +1%, which doesn't fit.

Consider the dollar's 12m change of +10.8: that is consistent with February-April 2015. For March 2015, the S&P returned -1.6% and the 10-year yield was 1.94%. A 1m return of -2.2% is close, and 7-10y Treasuries +1.6% fits March, when yields fell from 2.0 to 1.94... hmm, only about +0.6%. Payrolls in the data are perhaps as first reported (Mar 3m avg of 295, 264, 126 would be about 228). The snapshot's value of 287 is closer to the vintage in February (239, 329, 257 revised). Overall it is ambiguous, so I choose March 2015 with moderate confidence.
